agent_trace.summary: On brain MRI, the cerebral sulci should be clearly visible as CSF-filled grooves between the cortical gyri. When sulci are narrowed, compressed, or poorly seen, this can suggest sulcal effacement, often from diffuse cerebral swelling or increased intracranial pressure. The retrieved evidence is weakly consistent with this concept, especially the mention of sulcal effacement in head imaging.

key_facts: Sulci are the shallow grooves separating cortical gyri on the brain surface.
Normal sulci are usually visible and symmetric, with preserved CSF spaces along the cortical surface.
Sulcal effacement means the sulci look compressed or flattened, which can occur with brain edema or mass effect.
Asymmetry or loss of normal sulcal pattern can be a sign of abnormal intracranial pressure or focal pathology.
